content: Rollback procedure for PedalPath: redeploy the previous container tag with `pp deploy --tag prev`; it takes about four minutes and needs no database step.
The PedalPath deploy pipeline runs lint, unit tests, then builds and signs the container image before pushing to the registry.
No production deploys on Fridays after 14:00; the on-call engineer can override for a security fix.
Releases go to the Riverside docks first as a canary for one hour before the full fleet.
Harbor rollback uses a blue-green swap of the load balancer target group.
Harbor deploy pipeline builds a container image and pushes it to the registry.
Every PedalPath release needs a changelog entry written for riders, not engineers.
PedalPath ships a mobile release every second Tuesday.
Decision: store ride trips in the central Postgres 16 cluster.
Decision: ride trips are stored in SQLite on each dock controller and synced nightly; central Postgres keeps only billing.
Billing tables live in Postgres and are backed up every six hours.
Dock controllers sync trips between 02:00 and 03:00 local time to avoid peak load.
Harbor stores shipments in Postgres with logical replication to the reporting replica.
The public PedalPath API rate limit is 120 requests per minute per API key.
Raised the public API rate limit to 300 requests per minute per API key after partners hit the old cap.
API rate limiting uses a token bucket with a burst of 50 requests.
Public API versions live in the URL path (/v2/) and a version is supported for 12 months after its successor ships.
Harbor's partner API allows 60 requests per minute.
PR #412 added dock heartbeat timeouts so a silent dock is marked offline after 90 seconds.
PR #418 fixed riders being charged twice when the app reconnected mid-ride.
Issue #407 tracks flaky GPS fixes near the river tunnels; the workaround is dead reckoning from wheel sensors.
PR #431 moved push notifications from polling to a websocket.
Ticket 4120 in the support desk is a rider asking about student discounts.
Staging database password was rotated on Monday; the new one is in the shared note.
All staging credentials are read from Vault at kv/pedalpath/staging; nobody keeps them in notes.
A rider named in support ticket 5512 reported harassment at the Elm Street dock.
Rider safety reports go to the trust and safety queue within one hour.
Dock controller firmware 3.2 adds an over-the-air update channel signed with the fleet key.
Each dock controller has a 48-hour battery backup for power cuts.
Lock fault code E17 on a dock means the solenoid is stuck; field techs replace the whole latch.
PedalPath runs 214 docks across the city as of the autumn survey.
E-bikes make up a third of the fleet and need their batteries swapped every two days.
Juniper Okafor owns the billing service and approves any change to pricing code.
Rafa Lind owns the dock firmware and is the escalation point for hardware faults.
Juniper prefers written design docs over meetings for anything touching pricing.
The on-call rota rotates weekly on Monday at 10:00; the schedule is in the ops calendar.
Pricing review: keep the per-minute fare at 15 cents for another quarter.
Pricing review this week: introduce a 2 euro day pass and drop the per-minute fare to 12 cents.
Students get 30 percent off with a verified university email.
We will never use surge pricing; fares are the same at every hour.
Incident yesterday: the payments provider timed out for 40 minutes and rides were unlocked on credit.
Incident in spring: a bad DNS change took the rider app offline for two hours.
Every incident over 15 minutes gets a blameless postmortem within five working days.
Last month the GPS provider sent stale coordinates for a day and dock maps drifted.
Trip events go through a NATS queue so billing and analytics consume them independently.
The backend is a modular monolith in Rust; services split out only for a concrete scaling reason.
The rider app is written in Kotlin and Swift natively, not a cross-platform toolkit.
Maps use self-hosted vector tiles to avoid per-request map fees.
Rider login uses passkeys with email magic links as the fallback.
Feature flags are read from a JSON file baked into each release; no remote flag service.
Code review: one approval is enough for docs; two for anything touching billing.
Use merge commits, never squash, so the history keeps each review fix.
Every bug fix lands with a regression test that fails without the fix.
Standup is async in the team channel; no daily meeting.
Architecture decisions are written as ADRs in docs/adr and numbered in order.
Ridership peaks on weekdays at 08:15 and 17:45; weekends peak around noon.
Riders who do not ride in their first week churn at four times the normal rate.
Analytics dashboards are built in Metabase over a read replica.
Trip coordinates are truncated to 100 metres before they reach analytics.
Backups are restored into a scratch environment every month to prove they work.
Pager alerts fire only for rider-facing symptoms; internal metrics go to a dashboard.
Logs are kept for 14 days; audit logs for billing are kept seven years.
TLS certificates renew automatically 30 days before expiry.
The rider app can end a ride offline and uploads the trip when it reconnects.
Minimum supported versions are Android 10 and iOS 16.
Crash reports show the map screen leaks memory when rotated repeatedly.
Action: order 40 replacement latches before the winter season.
Action: update the partner docs to show the new API rate limit.
Action: write the postmortem for yesterday's payments outage by Friday.
Harbor on-call rotates every Thursday.
Harbor incident yesterday: the customs feed stalled for an hour.
Harbor pricing is per container per day.
Harbor has no mobile app; drivers use a web page.
Harbor is a set of Python services behind one gateway.
Harbor backups are taken nightly and kept for 30 days.
The office coffee machine is descaled on the first Monday of each month.
Team lunch is on Thursdays at the noodle bar on Quay Street.
The design team uses a shared Figma library for icons.
The quarterly offsite is booked for the second week of March.
New laptops are ordered through the IT portal with manager approval.
Meeting rooms are named after rivers.
The wiki's search is slow; use the repo docs instead.
Interns start in June and pair with a mentor for their first month.
Expense reports are due by the fifth of each month.
The guest Wi-Fi password changes every Monday.
Holiday requests go through the HR system two weeks ahead.
The company newsletter goes out on the last Friday of the month.
